title: How Did Ancient Humans Discover Alcohol?

titles: How Did Ancient Humans Discover Alcohol?
The 10 Million Year History of Alcohol
Who Made the First Beer in History?
Why Do Humans Drink Alcohol? It Started With Apes
Ancient Alcohol: Drunk Apes, Beer Pay and Wine
seo.best_title: How Did Ancient Humans Discover Alcohol?
seo.description_hook: How did ancient humans discover alcohol? The story starts 10 million years before the first human, with an ape and a rotten fruit, and ends with workers paid in beer and a goddess saved by a beer prank.
paragraphs: In this animated history of alcohol we follow the drunken monkey hypothesis, the ancient gene change that made our ancestors 40 times better at processing alcohol, and wild chimpanzees in Guinea that drink fermented palm sap.

Then we visit the oldest known beer at Raqefet Cave, the beer-before-bread debate and Gobekli Tepe, a 9,000 year old drink from Jiahu in China, the first wine in Georgia and Armenia, honey mead, Sumerian beer straws, Hammurabi's tavern laws, and Egyptian pyramid workers paid in beer.

We finish with Nubians whose bones show traces of an antibiotic from their beer, Greek watered-down wine, Roman posca, Aztec pulque and Andean chicha, medieval monks and official ale tasters, and the popular myth that beer was drunk because water was unsafe.
sources: Carrigan et al. - Hominids adapted to metabolize ethanol long before human-directed fermentation, PNAS (2015)
Robert Dudley - The Drunken Monkey: Why We Drink and Abuse Alcohol (2014)
Hockings et al. - Tools to tipple: ethanol ingestion by wild chimpanzees, Royal Society Open Science (2015)
Liu et al. - Fermented beverage and food storage in 13,000 y-old stone mortars at Raqefet Cave, Israel, J. Archaeological Science: Reports (2018)
Braidwood et al. - Did Man Once Live by Beer Alone? American Anthropologist (1953)
McGovern et al. - Fermented beverages of pre- and proto-historic China, PNAS (2004)
McGovern et al. - Early Neolithic wine of Georgia in the South Caucasus, PNAS (2017)
Barnard et al. - Chemical evidence for wine production around 4000 BCE in the Late Chalcolithic Near Eastern highlands, J. Archaeological Science (2011)

Nelson et al. - Brief communication: Mass spectroscopic characterization of tetracycline in the skeletal remains of an ancient population from Sudanese Nubia 350-550 CE, Am. J. Physical Anthropology (2010)

shots.say: Right now, millions of people around the world are holding a drink.
Some of them are a little bit drunk. Some are just getting started.
Maybe you had one last weekend. Beer, wine, whatever.
You didn't think about it. You drank it, and you moved on.
But that drink is one of the oldest habits our species has.

shots.title: OLDER THAN...
shots.say: It's older than writing. Older than cities. Probably older than farming.
Actually, it's older than human beings themselves.
Because this story starts about ten million years ago.
With an ape, a hot afternoon, and a piece of rotten fruit.
shots.ai: an ape-like stick figure sitting in a jungle holding an overripe fruit

shots.say: So, when did our ancestors start drinking? And why did they keep going?

shots.title: TODAY
shots.say: Today: drunk apes, the first brewers, workers paid in beer, and a very drunk goddess.
Grab a drink if you like. Let's go.

shots.say: Picture a forest millions of years ago. Fruit everywhere.
shots.ai: a lush prehistoric forest full of fruit trees

shots.say: When fruit gets very ripe, it starts to rot.

shots.title: HOW FRUIT MAKES ALCOHOL
shots.say: Tiny yeasts eat the sugar inside, and turn it into alcohol.
That's fermentation. It happens all by itself.
Nobody invented alcohol. Nature was making it long before us.
And animals found it. Birds, bats, insects, monkeys.
shots.ai: birds and a monkey eating fallen fermented fruit under a tree

shots.say: Why would an animal eat rotting fruit?

shots.title: BECAUSE
shots.say: Because it's sweet, full of energy, and the smell carries a long way.
A biologist called Robert Dudley came up with a fun idea about this.
shots.label: ROBERT DUDLEY

shots.say: He called it the drunken monkey hypothesis.

shots.title: THE IDEA
shots.say: Apes that followed the smell of alcohol found more ripe fruit, and survived better.
Other scientists aren't fully convinced. But it's a great theory.

Apes that followed the smell of alcohol found more ripe fruit, and survived better. Other scientists aren't fully convinced. But it's a great theory.

shots.say: Here's the part with real evidence. It's in our DNA.

shots.title: YOUR BODY
shots.say: Your body uses an enzyme to break down alcohol.
In 2015, scientists rebuilt this enzyme from our ancient ancestors.
They found that about ten million years ago, it changed.
After the change, our ancestors got around forty times better at handling alcohol.
That's around the time our ancestors spent more time on the ground.
shots.ai: an early ape ancestor walking on the forest floor picking up fallen fruit

shots.say: And fruit on the ground is the ripest, most fermented fruit of all.
So our ancestors evolved to handle a drink before they evolved to stand up straight.
Without that change, even a little alcohol would have hit us much harder.
So when someone says they can handle their drinks, thank a ten million year old ape.

shots.say: And our closest living relatives? Some of them still do this.

shots.label: GUINEA
shots.say: In Guinea, in West Africa, scientists watched wild chimpanzees for years.
Local people tap palm trees and collect the sweet sap in containers.
shots.ai: a palm tree with a container tied to it collecting sap in a West African forest

shots.say: The sap ferments quickly into a weak palm wine.
The chimps climbed up, chewed leaves into little sponges, and dipped them in.
shots.ai: a chimpanzee in a palm tree dipping a leaf sponge into a container of palm wine

shots.say: The drink was about three percent alcohol, like a light beer.
Some chimps drank a lot. A few showed signs of being drunk.
Some got sleepy. Some got restless.
So the habit is old. Very old. But apes didn't make their own drinks.
For that, we need humans. And a lot of grain.

shots.say: Fast forward to about thirteen thousand years ago.

shots.label: RAQEFET CAVE
shots.say: In a cave in what is now Israel, called Raqefet Cave.
A group called the Natufians used it to bury their dead.
shots.ai: stick figures in fur clothes gathered quietly in a cave with a small fire

shots.say: They were hunter-gatherers. Not yet farmers.
In the cave floor, archaeologists found deep holes carved into the rock.
shots.label: STONE MORTARS

shots.title: THE RECIPE?
shots.say: Inside were traces of wheat and barley that had been soaked, heated, and fermented.
That's beer. Probably the oldest beer we've found.
Not beer like today. More like a thick, sour porridge.
Lumpy, warm, and full of bits. Delicious.
They may have drunk it at funeral feasts, to honour the dead.
To be fair, some researchers question whether it really was beer.
But it's the oldest strong clue we have so far.

shots.say: Which leads to one of the biggest arguments in archaeology.
But here's the weird part.
Why did humans start farming in the first place?
Farming is hard. Hunting and gathering is often easier.
Early farmers worked longer and were often less healthy than hunter-gatherers.
In 1953, scientists held a debate with an amazing title.

shots.text: DID MAN ONCE LIVE BY BEER ALONE?
shots.say: Did man once live by beer alone?

shots.title: THE BEER THEORY
shots.say: The idea: maybe people first grew grain to make beer, not bread.

shots.label: GOBEKLI TEPE
shots.say: At Gobekli Tepe in Turkey, people built huge stone monuments over eleven thousand years ago.
Archaeologists found giant stone tubs there. Some think they held beer for feasts.
shots.label: STONE TUBS
shots.ai: huge ancient stone vats at Gobekli Tepe with carved stone pillars

shots.say: So civilization might have started with a party. And a lot of beer.
Other experts say bread came first, and beer was a side project.
Honestly, we don't know yet. But it's the best argument in history.

shots.label: JIAHU
shots.say: Now jump to China, to a village called Jiahu.
About nine thousand years ago.
People there buried pottery jars. Inside them, scientists found chemical traces.
shots.ai: ancient Chinese pottery jars in a neolithic village

shots.title: THE INGREDIENTS
shots.say: Rice, honey, and fruit, like hawthorn or grapes.
A fermented mix of all three. One of the oldest known drinks.
A researcher named Patrick McGovern studies these drinks. People call him Doctor Pat.
shots.label: DR. PAT

shots.say: He even worked with a brewery to recreate the Jiahu drink.
So yes, you can buy a version of a nine thousand year old drink.
And Jiahu is also famous for something else. Bone flutes.
Music and drinks. Some things never change.

shots.say: Beer and mixed drinks came early. But what about wine?

shots.label: GEORGIA
shots.say: For that, we go to the mountains of Georgia, between Europe and Asia.
Around eight thousand years ago, people there made wine in big clay jars.
Some jars were decorated with bunches of grapes.
shots.ai: large ancient clay jars decorated with grape patterns in the Caucasus mountains

shots.say: Basically, the first wine labels.

shots.label: ARMENIA
shots.say: Next door in Armenia, in a cave called Areni-1...
...archaeologists found a complete winery about six thousand years old.

shots.title: ARENI WINERY
shots.say: A basin for stomping grapes with feet, and jars to ferment the juice.
Yes. Feet. The original wine press was your neighbor's feet.
They also found cups, and burials nearby. Wine was probably used at ceremonies.

shots.say: There's another very old drink that needs no farming at all.
Mead. Wine made from honey.

shots.title: HOW MEAD HAPPENS
shots.say: Mix honey with water, leave it alone, and wild yeast does the rest.
Honey that got rained on could ferment all by itself.
So some people think mead could be one of humanity's oldest drinks.
Honestly, it's hard to prove. Honey leaves very few traces.
Later, mead became famous in northern Europe.
shots.ai: two fur-clad northern European stick figures toasting with mugs of mead by a fire

shots.say: Big halls, long winters, and a lot of honey wine.
The Greeks drank honey wine too. They called it hydromel. Honey water.
Which sounds healthy. It was not health food.

shots.label: SUMER
shots.say: Then came the first cities, in Mesopotamia.
And the Sumerians? They loved beer.

shots.label: GODIN TEPE
shots.say: At a site called Godin Tepe in Iran, a jar over five thousand years old still had beer residue.
Sumerian beer was cloudy, with floating husks.
shots.label: CLOUDY BEER

shots.say: So they drank it through long straws, from a shared jar.
shots.ai: two Sumerian stick figures sitting on either side of a big jar drinking through long straws

shots.say: The first straws in history were for beer.
They even had a goddess of beer. Her name was Ninkasi.
A hymn to Ninkasi, written down almost four thousand years ago, describes making beer.
shots.label: HYMN TO NINKASI

shots.say: It's a song and a recipe at the same time.

shots.title: BEER = PAY
shots.say: Workers were often paid partly in beer and bread.
Beer wasn't just a party drink. It was food, payment, and a gift to the gods.

Workers were often paid partly in beer and bread. Beer wasn't just a party drink. It was food, payment, and a gift to the gods.

shots.say: Where there's beer, there are taverns. And where there are taverns, there are rules.
Around seventeen fifty-four B C, King Hammurabi of Babylon wrote his famous laws.
Some of them are about taverns.
shots.label: HAMMURABI

shots.say: Taverns were often run by women, called alewives.
shots.ai: a Babylonian tavern keeper serving beer from a large jar

shots.say: If a tavern keeper cheated customers on the price of beer...
...the law said she could be thrown into the river.
That's a very harsh review.
Another law said she had to report criminals who met in her tavern.
So the first bartender was also part-time police.

shots.label: EGYPT
shots.say: In ancient Egypt, beer was everywhere.
Rich or poor, young or old. Everyone drank it.
Even the people who built the pyramids.
shots.ai: stick figure workers dragging stone blocks near a pyramid under the hot sun

shots.say: And no, they weren't slaves. Most were paid workers.

shots.title: DAILY PAY
shots.say: Their pay included bread, beer, and other food.
Some estimates say a worker could get around four liters of beer a day.
Four liters? Every day? How did anything get built?
Because this beer was weak, thick, and full of calories.
More like liquid bread than a party drink.
Hot sun, hard work, and a big jug of beer at the end of the day.
Honestly, not the worst job benefits in history.

Honestly, not the worst job benefits in history.

shots.say: The Egyptians even had a myth where beer saved humanity.
The sun god Ra was angry with people. They had stopped respecting him.
shots.label: RA

shots.say: So he sent a goddess to punish them. Her name was Sekhmet.
shots.label: SEKHMET
shots.ai: a fierce lion-headed goddess silhouette rampaging across the Egyptian desert

shots.say: Sekhmet went too far. She wanted to destroy everyone.
Ra changed his mind. But how do you stop an unstoppable goddess?

shots.title: RA'S PLAN
shots.say: He ordered thousands of jars of beer, dyed red to look like blood.
The red beer was poured across the fields at night.
shots.ai: jars of red beer flooding the fields at night in ancient Egypt

shots.say: Sekhmet woke up, saw a lake of red, and drank all of it.
She got so drunk she fell asleep. Humanity was saved.
Saved by a beer prank.
Egyptians even held a festival to remember it. The Festival of Drunkenness.
Yes, that was its real name. Ancient Egypt did not do subtle.

shots.label: NUBIA
shots.say: Just south of Egypt, in ancient Nubia, scientists found something amazing.
They studied bones of people buried almost two thousand years ago.
shots.label: NUBIAN BONES

shots.say: Under a special light, the bones glowed.
The glow came from tetracycline. An antibiotic.
Antibiotics were only discovered in the twentieth century.

shots.title: THE THEORY
shots.say: The best explanation: their beer was brewed with grain that grew antibiotic-making bacteria.
So they may have been drinking a mild antibiotic. Regularly. Since childhood.
Did they know it worked? We don't know. But it might have kept them healthier.
Please do not try this with your local beer. It does not work like that.

shots.label: GREECE
shots.say: Over in Greece, wine was king.
Greeks held drinking parties called symposia. Mostly men, lying on couches.
shots.ai: Greek men in togas reclining on couches at a symposium with wine cups

shots.say: They talked about philosophy, told jokes, sang, and played games.
But here's the rule: you never drank wine straight.

shots.title: GREEK WINE
shots.say: Wine was mixed with water in a big bowl, often more water than wine.
Drinking it unmixed was considered wild. Something only barbarians did.
Imagine telling an ancient Greek about tequila shots.
They also thought beer was a foreigner's drink. Very snobby.

shots.label: ROME
shots.say: The Romans took wine and made it an industry.
Wine for rich people. Cheap wine for poor people.
Huge clay jars carried wine across the whole empire.
Shipwrecks full of wine jars still sit on the bottom of the Mediterranean.
shots.ai: an ancient Roman shipwreck on the seabed full of clay amphorae

shots.say: Soldiers drank something called posca. Sour wine mixed with water.
Basically vinegar water. Refreshing? Debatable.
And beer? The Romans looked down on it too. A drink for northern tribes.
Which is funny, because a lot of those northern places are famous for beer today.

shots.say: Meanwhile, on the other side of the world, people invented their own drinks.

shots.label: CENTRAL MEXICO
shots.say: In Mexico, people made pulque from the sap of the agave plant.
It's milky white, a little sour, and gently alcoholic.
shots.label: PULQUE
shots.ai: a large agave plant with a jar of milky pulque beside it in central Mexico

shots.say: The Aztecs had strict rules about it.
Getting drunk in public could be punished very harshly.
But one Aztec manuscript shows an exception. The elderly.
shots.ai: two elderly Aztec stick figures happily drinking pulque

shots.say: Reach old age, and you've earned your drink.

shots.label: ANDES
shots.say: In the Andes, people drank chicha, a beer made from corn.
And to start it fermenting, people chewed the corn first.

shots.title: CHICHA
shots.say: Saliva turns starch into sugar, and the sugar becomes alcohol.
Gross? Yes. Clever chemistry? Also yes.
Chicha was so important that Inca rulers served it at huge state feasts.

shots.say: Jump to medieval Europe. Beer was part of daily life.
Breakfast, lunch, dinner. Ale was on the table.
But most of it was small beer. Very weak.
Even children drank it sometimes. It was more like a snack in a cup.
Monasteries brewed some of the best beer around.
shots.ai: medieval monks brewing beer in a monastery courtyard

shots.say: They sold it to support the monastery, and to feed travelers.
Towns even hired official beer testers, called ale-conners.
shots.label: ALE-CONNER
shots.ai: a serious medieval official tasting a mug of ale in a market

shots.say: Professional beer taster. Paid by the town. Dream job.
Their job was to make sure ale was good, and sold at a fair price.

shots.say: Now, you've probably heard this one before.
People in the past drank beer because the water was dirty.
Sounds logical. Boiling, alcohol, germs. Right?
Many historians say this is mostly a myth.
People drank plenty of water. From wells, springs, and rivers.
shots.ai: a medieval villager drinking water from a well

shots.say: Beer was popular because it was food, it gave energy, and it tasted good.
Also, people liked being a bit tipsy. Some things are simple.
And everything we've talked about so far was fairly weak.

shots.title: HOW STRONG?
shots.say: Rotten fruit, beer, wine. Strong spirits came much later.
Distilling strong alcohol spread in Europe about eight hundred years ago.
Monks and doctors called it water of life. Medicine, supposedly.

Distilling strong alcohol spread in Europe about eight hundred years ago. Monks and doctors called it water of life. Medicine, supposedly.

shots.title: THE STORY
shots.say: From rotten fruit, to cave beer, to clay jars, to bar laws, to today.
So, when did humans start drinking? Before we were even human.
Our bodies were shaped by it. Our parties were built on it.
Maybe even farming itself started with a drink.
So next time you raise a glass, remember who you're copying.
An ape with a rotten fruit. A Natufian in a cave. An Egyptian on payday.
Cheers to them.
But there's one thing ancient drinkers had to deal with the next morning.
The hangover.
And their cures were wild. Some involved owls.
That's the next video. Trust me, you'll want to see it.
